analysis.one_liner: Requires USDA to set nutrition standards for all junk food and drinks sold in schools outside of school meals.
analysis.headline: Backed by 172 House cosponsors, the bill was referred to a subcommittee in April 2009 and never got a hearing, markup, or vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal school lunches must meet nutrition standards, but food sold on the side — vending machines, cafeteria snack lines, school stores, snack bars — does not, and the last national standard for those items dated to 1979. This bill would have directed the Agriculture Department to write new science-based nutrition standards for all food sold on school campuses during the school day, with a possible limited exemption for infrequent school fundraisers, and to update the standards whenever the federal Dietary Guidelines are revised. It was introduced in March 2009, sent to a House subcommittee, and never acted on again.
analysis.who_benefits: Schoolchildren and their parents gain: every snack and drink sold anywhere on campus during the school day would have to meet standards based on current nutrition science, instead of rules written in 1979. Federal taxpayers also gain indirectly, since the bill's stated aim was to protect the federal investment in school meals from being undercut by competing junk food sales.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Secretary of Agriculture to establish science-based nutrition standards for all foods sold outside the school meal programs, on the school campus, at any time during the extended school day — covering vending machines, a la carte cafeteria sales, school stores, and snack bars.

In setting the standards, the Secretary must consider recommendations from authoritative scientific organizations and evidence on how nutrients, sodium, saturated and trans fats, and added sugars affect children's diets and rates of overweight, obesity, and chronic illness.

The standards must be reviewed and updated whenever USDA and HHS publish a new edition of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, so they track current science rather than freezing at 1979 definitions of 'food of minimal nutritional value.'

The bill's findings state that childhood obesity rates tripled since the 1970s, children's sodium intake is 214 percent above recommended levels, and the estimated national cost of obesity is $123 billion a year, half of it paid through Medicare and Medicaid.

analysis.who_pays: Snack food and beverage makers lose a school sales channel: sodas, candy, chips, and other items failing the new standards could no longer be sold on campus during the school day. Schools and student groups that depend on vending commissions, a la carte sales, and fundraising revenue would bear some of that loss, though the bill directs the Secretary to allow limited exemptions for infrequent, school-approved fundraisers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Snack and beverage vendors; school fundraisers

drawbacks.text: Schools and parent groups often fund activities, teams, and equipment with vending commissions, a la carte sales, and fundraiser proceeds; new nutrition standards would cut into that revenue, and the bill only offers a possible limited exemption for infrequent school-approved fundraisers, leaving the details to the Secretary.

The bill replaces the existing 1979 'food of minimal nutritional value' framework with standards written entirely by the Secretary of Agriculture through regulation, which shifts the specific rules from Congress to regulators and would require schools and vendors to adapt to a new set of requirements after a public rulemaking process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a nationwide upgrade of school nutrition rules that had not been updated since 1979, aimed directly at children's health and at protecting the federally subsidized school meal program from competing junk food sales. The costs are real but modest and targeted: reduced snack and soda sales revenue for vendors, schools, and student fundraisers, with a limited exemption mechanism available for fundraisers. The design is straightforward and delegates the technical standard-setting to USDA, which is a reasonable choice for a rule that must track changing science.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to its subcommittee on Healthy Families and Communities in April 2009, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Woolsey introduced the bill on March 5, 2009, with 89 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
On April 29, 2009, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Healthy Families and Communities, which was its last action of record.

Despite 172 cosponsors — 169 House Democrats and 3 House Republicans — the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Snack food and beverage sellers kept unrestricted access to school vending machines, stores, and cafeteria snack lines under the 1979 rules, since no new standards were ever written. Schoolchildren got nothing from the two years the bill sat in subcommittee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Snack and beverage sellers in schools

for.name: Rep. Lynn Woolsey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 89 original cosponsors and led it as its House sponsor.

for.name: 169 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-caucus support in the House.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Healthy Families and Communities
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 29, 2009 and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Standing committee with jurisdiction over child nutrition
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from referral on March 5, 2009 onward without ever voting it out to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic: 169 of 253 House Democrats cosponsored, versus 3 of 178 House Republicans, and no vote ever took place.

industries.industry: Snack food and beverage makers selling into schools
industries.note: The bill subjects everything they sell on campus during the school day — vending machine drinks, a la carte snacks, school store items — to science-based nutrition standards, which would force sodas, candy, and other products out or off the menu. Their interest in keeping the 1979-era rules ran against the bill's child-health purpose.

industries.industry: School food service and school meal programs
industries.note: The bill's stated purpose is to protect the federal investment in school lunch and breakfast programs from being undercut by unregulated competitive food sales, so reimbursed school meals would face less competition from junk food sold in the same building.

industries.industry: School fundraisers and student activity groups
industries.note: These groups depend on selling food to raise money, and new standards could cut into that revenue; the bill partially offsets this by directing the Secretary to allow limited exemptions for infrequent, school-approved fundraisers.
